e.t: Bocheru is a Hebrew personal name, preserved in English as “Bocheru” rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles. As a name, it identifies a particular person in the genealogical record; its exact significance or any underlying wordplay cannot be established from the available information. The name appears in 1 Chronicles 8:38 and 1 Chronicles 9:44.

Adbeel is a personal name used to identify a person in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is not presented here as a word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is best understood as the person’s name rather than as a translated description. It occurs twice in the Hebrew corpus, at Genesis 25:13 and 1 Chronicles 1:29, and is rendered “Adbeel” in both passages. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to a building or constructed structure. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Ezekiel 41:13, and its repeated rendering there is “building.” As a noun, it identifies the structure itself rather than an action or quality. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a building considered as a completed or established structure.

Birsha is a personal name, rendered “Birsha.” It identifies one individual in the Hebrew Old Testament and does not function as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once, in Genesis 14:2. Because no short definition or broader lexical sense is available here, its secure meaning for a reader is its naming function: it identifies Birsha as a person. The surrounding verse determines his role in that passage, but the name itself primarily serves as a personal designation.

This Hebrew word expresses desire—a longing or wish for something. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job 34:36, so its normal meaning is supported by a single occurrence rather than a broad range of passages. The word functions as an expression of what someone wants or wishes for. Its precise force in Job depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are needed to explain how that desire operates there.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “sinews,” the body tissues that connect and support parts of the body. It is used seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including descriptions of the human body and prophetic imagery involving bones. As a noun, it identifies a physical bodily part rather than an action or quality. Its exact force in any verse is determined by the surrounding passage.

Gilalai is a personal name used to identify an individual in Nehemiah 12:36. It is not presented with an explicit definition describing an action, quality, or object; its function is naming rather than describing. This Hebrew word occurs once in the Hebrew corpus, so its supported meaning is limited to the name itself. The precise role of the named individual depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

The word can therefore describe both a literal planted space and a setting associated with beauty, provision, or abundance. It occurs 42 times in the Old Testament, from Genesis through Joel, and is also connected with creation, command, movement, speech, and judgment in the scriptural evidence.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Deborah.” It identifies people rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs ten times, appearing once in Genesis and repeatedly in Judges. The name is associated with individuals who are named in the surrounding scriptural accounts, including references connected with death, speech, and giving. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding context, but its ordinary function is as a woman’s personal name.

This Hebrew word refers to an action or condition in Jeremiah 14:9, but its precise meaning cannot be determined from the available lexical information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, making its normal usage impossible to compare across multiple passages. The reference identifies where it occurs, but without the verse text or an explicit definition, no more specific meaning can be stated responsibly.

This Hebrew word refers to “records,” functioning as a noun for information preserved for later consultation. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Ezra, across two verses. Its use points to recorded material that can be consulted when documenting or checking matters. The exact force in either Ezra passage depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to "thistles," a troublesome kind of plant. It is a noun used for vegetation found in the field and appears only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament: once in Genesis 3:18 and once in Hosea 10:8. Its normal sense is therefore a prickly or unwanted plant, rather than an action or quality. The exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies this type of vegetation.

Hodaiah is a Hebrew personal name used to identify an individual, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in 1 Chronicles 3:24, within a genealogical list. Because the available rendering presents it as a name and no lexical definition is supplied, its ordinary meaning here is its identifying function: it names a person. The surrounding verse text would be needed to say anything further about that individual or the name’s contextual significance.

This Hebrew verb means “praise”: it expresses honoring or exalting someone, especially in worship directed toward God. It can describe an action commanded of people, a public response, or words and song offered in worship. The word occurs 165 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it has broad use rather than referring to one isolated setting. Its relationships with God, worship, singing, and joyful expression reinforce its normal function as an active call or response of praise.

Zabbai is a Hebrew personal name, used to identify an individual rather than to express an action, quality, or object. It appears twice in the Old Testament corpus, once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. Since the available English rendering preserves it as the name “Zabbai,” the word’s ordinary meaning is its role as a person’s name. The particular identity and significance of the person must be determined from the surrounding passage, not from the name itself.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. Its precise English meaning cannot be stated confidently here because no definition or approved meaning term is available. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with occurrences in Daniel 5:19 and Daniel 6:26. Those references identify where it occurs, but without the verse text they do not establish the word’s specific force in either passage. Its meaning should therefore be understood from the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew verb means “sing.” It describes the act of singing and is used prominently in worshipful language connected with the LORD. The word occurs 45 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, with most occurrences in Psalms. Its indexed uses also connect singing with God’s name, God’s works, and judgment, showing that it can express a verbal response to who God is and what he does. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name: “Hushai.” It identifies a person in the Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. The name appears 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mostly in 2 Samuel, and is consistently rendered “Hushai.” Its occurrences connect with speech, counsel, meeting, and worship-or-bowing events, showing that it functions as a person’s name within narrative passages. The precise significance of each occurrence comes from its surrounding verse and passage.

This Hebrew word expresses the meaning “good.” It functions as the sentence’s predicate, stating something about the people or subject being described. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Ecclesiastes 12:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, since the available lexical information is limited. The word is therefore best understood at its basic level as a term describing goodness or favorable quality, without extending it into a more specific idea not established here.

Harosheth is the name of a specific place. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Judges 4, where the English rendering preserves the name as “Harosheth.” The word itself does not provide a broader meaning in the available passages, so its ordinary lexical sense is simply this geographical name. Its precise significance in any one occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: Ahihud is a personal name, rendered “Ahihud.” It does not have an explicit definition in the available lexical material, so it is best understood as the name of an individual rather than as a description or action. The name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 8:7. Its occurrence is associated with a genealogy and with a birth or begetting relationship, identifying it within a family record. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the individual’s specific role there.

This Hebrew word means “shot.” It functions as an action word describing the act of shooting, rather than naming a person, object, or place. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis 21:16. The surrounding verse determines the exact subject and circumstances of the shooting, but the word itself points plainly to that action. Its recorded use is connected with relationships involving a voice and a bow, reinforcing the sense of an action carried out by shooting.

“Jahdiel” is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Hebrew Bible, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 5:24. The available English renderings preserve it as “Jahdiel,” so its primary function is to name the person mentioned in that passage. Without the surrounding verse text, no further contextual meaning should be assigned to the name itself.

Jakeh is a personal name, referring to a person named “Jakeh,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs only once, in Proverbs 30:1. The name itself does not explain the person’s identity, character, or role; those details must come from the surrounding passage and broader biblical context, not from the name alone.

e.t: This word functions as “The,” pointing to a particular person, thing, or idea. It serves a defining role in a sentence rather than expressing an action or describing a quality. The word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across books including Deuteronomy, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes. Its precise force in any sentence depends on the noun or expression it helps identify.

This Hebrew word means “tree,” referring to a woody plant. It functions as a noun and is used six times in the Hebrew Bible, all in Daniel 4. The word identifies the prominent tree seen in Nebuchadnezzar’s dream and mentioned repeatedly as the dream is recounted and explained. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a tree, understood as a physical plant within the passage’s imagery. The surrounding verse and larger account determine what the tree represents in that specific setting.

This Hebrew verb means “removed.” It functions as a verb, stating that its subject is described as removed rather than naming a person, object, or place. In the Hebrew Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Isaiah 30:20. That single occurrence establishes its basic lexical sense, while the exact force of the word within that specific sentence depends on the surrounding Hebrew sentence and its subject.

This Hebrew word means “heart.” It functions as a noun referring to the heart in its ordinary biblical use. In the Hebrew Old Testament data represented here, it occurs seven times, all in Daniel, and is consistently rendered “heart.” Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the heart. Scripture references include Daniel 2:30, 4:16, 5:20–22, and 7:4.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information alone. It occurs once in the Hebrew Scriptures, in Ezra 4:12, and no explicit definition or approved English meaning is available for it here. Its sense must therefore be determined from the actual verse and its surrounding passage, rather than from the word by itself.

Moreh functions as a proper place-name in the Hebrew Old Testament. It identifies a location rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. The word appears three times, in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and Judges, and is consistently rendered “Moreh.” Because no verse text or surrounding context is included here, the specific significance of the place in each passage must be determined from its context.

It occurs 60 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with many occurrences in Job. Its surrounding wording determines what is being said about God in each passage, but the central meaning remains God.

This Hebrew noun means “breeches,” referring to a garment worn on the lower body. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in passages concerning priestly clothing and related instructions. The word therefore identifies a specific item of clothing rather than an action, quality, or person. Its occurrences extend from Exodus through Ezekiel, showing its use in descriptions of sacred service and priestly dress.

This Hebrew noun means “bastard,” referring to a person identified by that designation. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 23:2 and Zechariah 9:6. In both passages, it functions as a specific description of a person or group rather than an action or quality expressed by a verb. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself carries this direct identifying sense.

e.t: Mephibosheth is a personal name, not an ordinary Hebrew word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it identifies a person and appears seventeen times, all in 2 Samuel. The name is preserved consistently as “Mephibosheth” in the available English renderings. Its occurrences connect with genealogical references, commands concerning him, speech about him, and acts of bowing before the king. The name itself therefore identifies the individual; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand what is being said or done concerning him.

This Hebrew noun means “fryingpan,” naming a cooking utensil. It appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in Leviticus: in Leviticus 2:7 and Leviticus 7:9. The word identifies the pan used in preparing the food mentioned in those passages, distinguishing the utensil from the offering or food itself. Its basic function is therefore concrete and practical: it names an object used for cooking. The surrounding passage supplies the details of how that utensil is involved in each offering instruction.

Meshobab is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Meshobab.” It identifies an individual in the Old Testament and does not provide enough information here to establish a broader ordinary meaning or describe an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 4:34. Its precise significance as a personal name cannot be determined from the available lexical information, so it is best understood simply as the individual’s name in that genealogy.

The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Bible, in two verses: twice in Isaiah 57:19 and once in Malachi 1:12. Its basic sense remains focused on fruit, while the surrounding sentence determines what kind of fruit or production is being discussed.

This Hebrew word means “drop.” It describes an action in which something falls or comes down in drops, functioning as a verb in a sentence. Its ordinary sense is connected with dropping rather than with a person, place, or object. It occurs 18 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Judges, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and Song of Solomon. The precise force in any verse depends on what is described as dropping there.

This Hebrew verb describes leaving something behind, abandoning it, or spreading out from a place. Its central idea is separation: people, armies, or things move away rather than remain together. In English Bible renderings, the approved dominant meaning is “spread,” while related uses can describe forsaking or being left. It occurs 40 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its exact force depends on what is being left or dispersed in each passage. The word can describe both deliberate departure and a condition of being scattered or abandoned.

Its uses consistently point to people assigned to transport or bear what is needed for a work or task. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “blindness,” the loss or absence of sight. It is used three times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, appearing in two passages: Genesis 19:11 and 2 Kings 6:18. In each occurrence, the word names blindness itself rather than describing a person, place, or action. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and account, but its central meaning remains straightforward: blindness or an inability to see.

In the Hebrew Bible, this form is represented once, at Daniel 4:31, so its use there is especially limited rather than broadly illustrated across many passages. e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “tribute”—a payment or offering given as an obligation. It names something presented to another party rather than an action or quality. Its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is a required payment presented to someone else.

This Hebrew word means “tenth,” identifying one portion out of ten. It is used for a measured share that may be given or taken, especially in passages concerning produce, increase, and a ruler’s claim. The word occurs nine times in the Old Testament, across seven verses, and its use includes the giving or taking of a tenth portion. Its exact role in a sentence depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “twenty,” a number used to identify a quantity of twenty items, people, measures, years, or other counted things. It appears 315 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its role is generally straightforward: it supplies a numerical value in statements about counts, ages, amounts, or dimensions. The surrounding noun or action determines what is being counted, while this word itself expresses the number twenty.

This Hebrew word means “lest.” It introduces a warning or precaution, pointing to an unwanted possibility that should be avoided. In a sentence, it connects an action, instruction, or concern with what might happen if that warning is ignored. It is used 133 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Malachi, serving this same cautionary function across many passages.

e.t: “Zophar” is a personal name, referring to a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears four times, all in the book of Job. The name is associated with speech in Job, where Zophar is presented as speaking and participating in the book’s conversations. Its occurrences are found in Job 2:11, 11:1, 20:1, and 42:9.

This Hebrew word means “small.” It functions as a description of something lesser in size or extent, with the specific thing being described determined by the surrounding sentence. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 101 times, showing that it is a recurring everyday description rather than a rare technical term. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what the word modifies there.

The word means “Arbite,” an identifying designation for a person. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 2 Samuel 23:35, and the available English renderings preserve it as “Arbite.” Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the term can be recognized as a personal designation, while the passage itself supplies any further detail about whom it identifies.

This Hebrew word refers to “hangings,” functioning as a noun for suspended coverings or enclosures. It is used especially in descriptions of the tabernacle courtyard, where hangings formed its surrounding boundary. The word occurs 22 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with many occurrences in Exodus while the courtyard and its construction are described. Its normal sense therefore points to hanging material used as part of an arranged structure, rather than to an action or abstract idea.

This Hebrew word means “first.” It identifies a person, thing, or event as preceding others in an order or sequence. It can mark what comes at the beginning, comes before something else, or holds the foremost place. The word occurs 182 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing broad use for describing priority and position rather than one narrow situation. Its exact force in a verse depends on what is being compared or arranged.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the place name “Rehoboth.” It identifies named locations in the Old Testament rather than describing an action or quality. It occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament: three times in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. In Genesis 26:22, it is connected with naming a place in the setting of spoken words. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain that passage more fully.

This Hebrew word means “paved.” It is a descriptive word that identifies something as having a paved surface. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Song of Solomon 3:10. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be explained further. Its basic sense remains a description of something paved, rather than an action, person, or abstract idea.

e.t: This word is a proper name rendered “Shobach.” It identifies an individual named in two Hebrew Old Testament occurrences, both in 2 Samuel 10. Because it functions as a name rather than a descriptive word, it does not express an action, quality, or object in ordinary translation. The name appears in 2 Samuel 10:16 and 10:18, with the later occurrence connected to a death event. Its precise role in each verse depends on the surrounding passage.

The Hebrew word means “consumption,” referring to something that consumes or wastes away. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Leviticus 26:16 and once in Deuteronomy 28:22. In both places, it names a condition or consequence described as consumption. The word’s precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a consuming, wasting effect rather than an ordinary act of eating.

Shisha is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea or action. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Kings 4:3, and is rendered “Shisha.” Because this word functions as a name, its meaning is primarily its identification of that person, not a description of character, conduct, or an abstract concept. The surrounding verse supplies the information needed to understand Shisha’s particular role there.

This Hebrew word means “amiss.” It marks something as not right or proper, serving as a brief description rather than naming a person, place, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 3:29. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the precise force of the word in that sentence must be understood from its context. Its basic sense remains a description of what is amiss.

“Shalman” is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Hosea 10:14. The name itself identifies the person; its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and cannot be determined from the name alone. This word should therefore be understood as a proper name, not translated as an ordinary descriptive term.

e.t: Ashur is a personal name, referring to a man named Ashur. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles, and is rendered “Ashur.” Its recorded uses belong to genealogical material: one identifies Ashur in a birth or begetting relationship, and another places him within the family record. Thus, this word functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the proper name “Simeon.” It identifies Simeon as a person and, in later passages, the tribal family associated with him. The name appears 44 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in genealogical lists and accounts of Israel’s tribes. Its use begins with Simeon’s birth and continues in references to his descendants and tribal identity. It functions as a name rather than a general description or action.

This Hebrew verb means to take property by force—to “plunder” or “rob.” It describes an action in which people or nations seize what belongs to others, often in the setting of conflict or oppression. The word occurs 11 times in the Old Testament corpus, including descriptions of enemies taking goods and armies gaining spoil. Its role is normally active: someone or a group performs the taking against another people or place. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is seized and who carries out the action.

This Hebrew word means “down.” It describes something being lowered, brought low, or moving toward a lower position. In the Old Testament, it is used 29 times, including passages about God bringing down the proud and exalting the humble. Its use as a sentence predicate shows that it expresses what happens to a person or thing: it becomes lower or is caused to go down. The surrounding context determines whether the lowering is physical or figurative.

This Hebrew word means “leave.” It functions as a verb, expressing an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 39:2. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself; the word’s basic lexical sense remains the action of leaving.

e.t: Tehinnah refers to a person named Tehinnah in a Hebrew genealogy. It functions as a personal name rather than as a common description or action. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in 1 Chronicles 4:12, within a record of family descent. Because no broader usage is recorded, its meaning is best understood as identifying this individual in that genealogy, rather than expressing a general idea used throughout Scripture.

The Hebrew word means “nether,” functioning as a positional term for identifying something in a lower place. It occurs 19 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in descriptions of locations, regions, and physical positions. Its use ranges from the structure of Noah’s ark to references involving the earth, waters, and the realm of the dead. The word therefore consistently marks what is situated in a lower position, while the surrounding passage determines the specific thing being described.

This Hebrew verb describes the action of making something “straight.” It functions as an action word rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Ecclesiastes, where it is rendered “straight.” Its use also appears in a statement describing what a teacher did, helping connect the word with arranging or presenting something in an orderly way. The surrounding verse determines the specific object being made straight.
